reading: The literature pass for the fault across the ring took about four minutes of wall time (18:49-18:53 on 5 November, searches run in parallel) against a 45-minute bound, sized to the values the study needs: restart times of common-mode failures in large distributed systems, space weather's effect on spacecraft electronics, fail-safe retrodirective beams, and formation-flying autonomy and sail attitude control. 'search summary' means the result summary of a web search, the document not opened; 'page' means the named web page was fetched and read for the stated facts; 'recalled' means general knowledge not checked here; 'via project' means a source the repository already reads, not re-read here. Nothing here is admitted as a manuscript source, and no outside bytes are kept.

sources.citation: 2024 CrowdStrike-related IT outages (Wikipedia), with CrowdStrike's Falcon Content Update Preliminary Post Incident Report and CISA's alert of 19 July 2024
sources.read: page (Wikipedia) for the times, the count and the recovery; the CrowdStrike report and CISA alert by search summary
used_for: a faulty content update released at 04:09 UTC on 19 July 2024 and reverted at 05:27 UTC, 78 minutes later
about 8.5 million Windows devices affected (Microsoft's estimate)
each machine had to be repaired locally, so recovery was expected to take days; Delta Air Lines returned to normal operations on 25 July, six days after the outage
precedent for a bad update across a fleet: the fix is fast, the restart slow when every unit needs local repair

sources.citation: D. Estevez, Galileo constellation outage (blog analysis, July 2019), with EUSPA/GSA notices as reported by Inside GNSS and others
sources.read: page for the start and the cause; the duration (about six days, over 80 hours by early reports) by search summary
used_for: service declared unavailable from 11-12 July 2019; restoration about six days later
cause: a failure of the Precise Timing Facility that generates Galileo System Time, which stopped the orbit and clock products, so the satellites broadcast stale ephemerides
precedent for a shared timing reference taking a whole constellation's service down for days

sources.citation: GPS World, 'GLONASS Gone . . . Then Back' and related reports of the 1-2 April 2014 GLONASS outage
used_for: illegal ephemerides uploaded to every satellite took effect simultaneously at about 21:00 UTC on 1 April 2014
the whole constellation broadcast corrupt data for about 11 hours and was unusable
precedent for a shared navigation upload corrupting every user's solution at once

sources.citation: Metsahovi Radio Observatory, GPS Time Disruptions on 26-Jan-2016 (Aalto University); RNTF case study of the 26 January 2016 GPS event
used_for: removing SVN 23 from service triggered a ground-software error that left 15 satellites' UTC offset wrong by about 13.7 microseconds
timing receivers jumped by 13 microseconds for about 12 hours; telecommunications and broadcasting were affected
precedent for a timing fault that leaves navigation intact while corrupting time

sources.citation: ThousandEyes, Starlink Outage Analysis: July 24, 2025; press reports of SpaceX's explanation
used_for: a global outage of about 2.5 hours from about 19:13 UTC on 24 July 2025
caused by the failure of internal software services of the core network during an upgrade of the ground compute clusters that host the constellation's control plane
precedent for a constellation's common control plane as a single point of failure, restored in hours

sources.citation: SentinelOne Labs, AcidRain: a modem wiper rains down on Europe (2022); Viasat statements as reported by Bleeping Computer and MIT Technology Review
used_for: on 24 February 2022 attackers used a misconfigured VPN appliance to reach KA-SAT's trusted management segment and issued legitimate management commands to many modems at once
the AcidRain wiper disabled the modems permanently; tens of thousands of customers across Europe lost service and Viasat shipped almost 30,000 modems to restore it
precedent for an intrusion that uses the system's own command authority, with a restart measured in weeks of hardware replacement

sources.citation: POWER Magazine, Understanding the April 2025 Iberian Peninsula Blackout; Wikipedia, 2025 Iberian Peninsula blackout
used_for: the whole Iberian grid blacked out at 12:33 local time on 28 April 2025
Spain re-energized 62% of substations in 9.5 hours and all in about 15.5; full load within about 24 hours; Portugal reconnected all load in about 12 hours
black start from hydro and gas plants: a large grid's restart takes about a day even with its sources intact

sources.citation: Solar particle induced upsets in the TDRS-1 attitude control system RAM during the October 1989 solar particle events (OSTI 131648); The magnitude and effects of extreme solar particle events, Space Weather and Space Climate 4 (2014)
used_for: three large solar particle events from 19 October 1989 lasted about six days at 1 AU
243 upsets in the RAM of TDRS-1's attitude control system during the events; upset rates on other craft rose from 1-2 a day to about 20
October 1989 underlies CREME96's worst-week and worst-day environments

sources.citation: NOAA, Service Assessment: Intense Space Weather Storms October 19 - November 07, 2003 (2004); NOAA Technical Memorandum OAR SEC-88
used_for: 17 major flares from 19 October to 5 November 2003
28 satellites reported anomalies and two were put out of service, among them ADEOS-II, lost after 24 October
precedent for space weather reaching many spacecraft at once over days

sources.citation: Lam et al., Anik-E1 and E2 satellite failures of January 1994 revisited, Space Weather 10 (2012)
used_for: on 20 January 1994 internal (bulk dielectric) charging and discharge disabled a part in the speed-control loop of both satellites' momentum wheels, the same day
Anik E1 was recovered in about seven hours on its backup wheel; Anik E2's backup could not be activated and its attitude recovery took many months
precedent for space weather disabling attitude control on several craft of one design at once

sources.citation: Galaxy 15 (Wikipedia); Spaceflight Now, January 2011; D. Ferguson et al., Plasma conditions during the Galaxy 15 anomaly and the possibility of ESD from subsurface charging (AIAA 2011)
used_for: Galaxy 15 stopped answering commands on 5 April 2010, probably after an electrostatic discharge, while its payload kept relaying
it drifted uncommanded for about nine months, a hazard to its neighbours, until its wheels saturated, it lost the Sun, its batteries drained and it rebooted on 27 December 2010
precedent for a transmitter that keeps radiating after control is lost: the beams must stop when they lose command or pilot

sources.citation: R. M. Dickinson (NASA), Microwave power transmission beam safety system, US patent 4,187,506 (filed 1978)
used_for: the beam's power, shape and direction are controlled from the pilot and from received, reflected and scattered power profiles
the system reshapes, dims or douses the beam when an object enters it, and withholds high power until the pilot profile shows an unobstructed path

the transmitter at about 10 kg per kW (as provisioning/energy_options.md carries it)

sources.citation: JAXA press release of 23 July 2010 on IKAROS attitude control; eoPortal, IKAROS; Y. Tsuda et al. on IKAROS's reflectivity control devices
used_for: 80 liquid-crystal reflectivity control devices at the sail's edge turned its Sun angle by about half a degree in 23 hours, about a degree a day, without propellant

the devices reflect specularly only while powered (via project: array_industry_sources, Mori et al.), so a trim that needs power to hold its state reverts when its power fails
